title: Number of 1 Bits
description: Brute force to optimized: checking all 32 positions versus Brian Kernighan's bit clearing trick.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, return the number of set bits (bits equal to 1) in its binary representation, sometimes called its Hamming weight.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Lit Switches on a Control Panel
blocks.text: Like counting how many switches on a row of 32 on-off switches are currently flipped to the "on" position, without needing to know their exact arrangement, just the total count.

blocks.caption: Count how many bits in the binary representation are set to 1

blocks.text: A value of 0 has no set bits anywhere in its binary representation, so the answer is 0.
It helps to ask whether every one of the 32 bit positions genuinely needs to be inspected, or whether work can be limited to just the bits that are actually set.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force checks all 32 fixed positions individually with a shift and a mask, doing the same amount of work whether n has zero set bits or all 32 set.

Observation 2: A number ending with several trailing zero bits gains nothing from being checked bit by bit; there is a direct arithmetic way to jump straight past those zeros.

Observation 3: Subtracting 1 from n flips every trailing zero bit to a 1 and flips the lowest set bit itself to 0, so ANDing n with n minus 1 always clears exactly that lowest set bit while leaving every bit above it untouched.

Observation 4: Tracing n = 11 (1011) confirms it, applying n AND (n minus 1) three times in a row clears the three set bits one at a time and reaches 0, so counting the iterations directly gives 3, without ever inspecting the 29 positions that were already 0.
Recognizing that n AND (n minus 1) always removes exactly one set bit is what turns a fixed 32 step scan into a loop that runs only as many times as there are set bits.
Check every one of the 32 bit positions individually, testing whether each one is set by shifting and masking, and count how many are.

items: For each of the 32 bit positions, isolate that bit using a mask.
If it is set, increment the count.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop always runs exactly 32 times regardless of n, since every bit position needs to be checked individually with no way yet to skip the zero ones.
An unsigned right shift is used so that a 1 bit shifted in from the left on some platforms cannot masquerade as a set bit at the wrong position.

blocks.text: Every one of the 32 possible bit positions is directly checked, so every set bit is correctly counted.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32), a fixed number of checks regardless of how many bits are actually set.
Space: O(1), only a counter is kept.
Limitation: this always performs all 32 checks even when n has very few set bits, when a technique exists that only performs as many steps as there are actual set bits.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it inspects all 32 fixed bit positions no matter how few of them are actually set.

What it wastes: every position holding a 0 still costs one shift and one mask, work that produces no useful information.

The key arithmetic fact: subtracting 1 from n turns its lowest set bit into 0 and every trailing zero bit below it into 1, so ANDing n with n minus 1 clears exactly that lowest set bit and nothing else.

The core idea: repeatedly clear the lowest set bit with n AND (n minus 1) and count how many times it takes to reach 0, since that count is exactly the number of set bits.

Use the identity that n AND (n minus 1) always clears exactly the lowest set bit of n, leaving every other bit unchanged. Repeating this operation and counting how many times it takes to reach 0 gives exactly the number of set bits, without ever needing to check positions that are already 0.
Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit using n AND (n minus 1), counting the iterations.

blocks.caption: Optimized: n and (n minus 1) clears the lowest set bit, count until n reaches 0

blocks.text: Each application of n AND (n minus 1) removes exactly one set bit and never removes or creates any other bit, so the number of iterations needed to reach 0 is exactly equal to the number of bits that were originally set.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["n has zero set bits (n = 0)","The loop condition is false immediately","Correctly returns 0 without ever entering the loop"],["n has k set bits","The loop runs exactly k times, clearing one bit per iteration","Correctly returns k"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of set bits), since the loop runs exactly once per set bit.
Space: O(1), only a counter is kept.

items: The loop condition checks n against 0 directly, so it naturally stops the moment every set bit has been cleared.
Each iteration performs one AND operation and one increment, with no wasted work on bit positions that are already 0.

blocks.text: The identity n AND (n minus 1) clearing the lowest set bit, known as Brian Kernighan's algorithm, is a foundational bit manipulation trick that reappears in many other problems involving counting or isolating set bits.

items: Using a signed right shift on a negative number in languages where that matters, which can shift in 1s instead of 0s and produce an infinite loop, when an unsigned shift should be used instead.
Forgetting that this technique's runtime depends on the number of set bits, not on 32, which matters when reasoning about its worst versus best case behavior.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n equal to 0","Zero set bits, the loop never executes at all."],["n with every bit set (all 1s in a 32 bit representation)","Takes the full 32 iterations, the worst case for this technique."]]}

blocks.text: Mention that many processors also provide a dedicated popcount hardware instruction that computes this in a single cycle, useful context to bring up when asked about further optimizing beyond the bit trick itself.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every bit position", think: n AND (n minus 1) to skip straight past unset bits.
If the interviewer says "is there hardware support for this", think: mention the popcount instruction available on modern processors.
If the interviewer says "what if n is negative", think: treat it as its 32 bit unsigned bit pattern, and use an unsigned shift if checking bit by bit.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(32) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (Brian Kernighan's algorithm): O(number of set bits) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Brian Kernighan's bit clearing trick, n AND (n minus 1), removing exactly the lowest set bit each iteration.
Core Idea: repeatedly clear the lowest set bit and count the iterations until n reaches 0.
Time: O(32) for the brute force, O(number of set bits) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: subtracting 1 from n always flips its lowest set bit and every trailing zero below it, making n AND (n minus 1) a precise way to remove exactly one set bit.
Interview Difficulty: the brute force is trivial; producing the Kernighan bit trick unprompted, with a correct explanation of why it works, is what stands out.
One line memory trick: n AND (n minus 1) clears the lowest set bit, count until n hits 0.
